new_statements.quote: While Mountain Ok languages are described as tonal (Telefol, Tifal, Mian), in Lowland Ok and Greater Awyu languages it is not the tone contour but lexical stress that seems to be distinctive.
new_statements.citation: van den Heuvel, Wilco & Sebastian Fedden. 2014. Greater Awyu and Greater Ok: Inheritance or Contact? Oceanic Linguistics 53(1): 1-36. doi:10.1353/ol.2014.0008 (open preprint/scan: HAL hal-03950196). [= A's work 5, now opened and read]
new_statements.locator: p. 2 (Oceanic Linguistics 53(1) pagination; PDF p. 3 of the HAL file), section 1 'The languages and their speakers', paragraph on phonology; cf. p. 18, sec. 6.2 'Typology'. scanned of these two pages saved as the PDF's own text layer is cut at the right margin but preserves '..in Lowland Ok and Greater Awyu lan|tour but lexical stress that seems to be distinctive.').
new_statements.check: not checked by the second reader
new_statements.relation_note: Family-level typological remark only: Mountain Ok languages (Telefol, Tifal, Mian) are tonal, whereas in Lowland Ok and Greater Awyu languages lexical (distinctive) stress rather than tone is contrastive; repeated on p. 18 for Muyu and Mandobo ('distinctive lexical stress, as is true for all other Awyu-Dumut languages and some other Ok languages'). No data or statement on Nakai; not usable as a Nakai stress statement, recorded so the family-level claim is held by the project.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule; claims stress (not tone) is the distinctive prosodic property in Lowland Ok and Greater Awyu, i.e. lexically contrastive stress, family-wide.
new_statements.exceptions: Mountain Ok (Telefol, Tifal, Mian) tonal; p. 18 limits the stress claim to 'all other Awyu-Dumut languages and some other Ok languages'.
new_statements.identity_note: Nakai [nkj] is not named anywhere in the paper (text layer + references searched; fig. 3 Ok tree = Ngalum, Muyu, Ninggerum, Yonggom, Mian, Faiwol, Tifal, Telefol, Bimin; 'Lowland Ok (Ngalum, K[ati]..) plus some languages not further considered here', p. 5). Glottolog cites it for Nakai only as the family-membership comment. The prosody sentence is a generalisation over 'Lowland Ok and Greater Awyu languages'; whether the authors would count the Tangko-Nakai/Central Ok varieties under it is not said, hence 'unclear' rather than 'yes'.

sources.note: Nothing on stress placement. Sec. 5.3 (pp. 9-11) treats Nakai (Burunggop, Awimbon) and Nagi (Tarngop, Kawor, Itutamon) as probably one language (63% lexical similarity); fn. 14: 'pronounced [naɣai] or [naʁai]'. Appendix B (p. 25) lexical-similarity rules: 'Unreleased consonants, accents and nasalized vowels are ignored.' Appendix C (pp. 26-34): Nagi/Tarngop (239 items) and Nakai/Awimbon (50 items) wordlists in IPA with primary-stress marks (ˈmitɔ 'nose', ˈkerkor 'mouth', semˈber 'fingernail'), mostly penultimate by rough tally; no analysis.
